cells.tense: The feeling is here now, settled and deep, and you sit with it before you move.
cells.act: go all the way into the pattern until you meet its edge
cells.ask: Take a hunch you've been carrying. Follow it into the pattern underneath, all the way to where your thinking runs out, and stay in that depth for a few minutes instead of turning back at the first tidy answer.
cells.core:
The feeling has settled into its own depth, and you sit with it before it has to choose. From that quiet you recognize what counts, and the recognition holds because you don't rush it into an answer. That's what makes the work feed you rather than take from you — the depth is the point, not a stage on the way to a conclusion.
There's more pattern under this than you've gone looking for. Take a hunch you've been carrying, follow it into what it's made of until you meet its edge, and stay in that depth for a few minutes instead of surfacing at the first tidy thought. What's freeing shows up at the edge, not before it.
cells.sheetLine: The feeling has depth, and you know how to sit in it.
cells.verb: sitting with what the heart knows before moving
cells.place: the quiet room where you recognize what matters before you can explain it

cells.tense: You are bracing for what comes next, holding the feeling open before it can settle.
cells.act: count what the ending gave you
cells.ask: Think of something that has finished, near or far. Before you reach ahead, count three things it gave you — small, specific, and yours.
cells.core:
You're holding the feeling open toward what comes next, keeping the depth ready before it has settled. The wait is happening at the future's edge, not in the water. Peace that keeps being held open becomes a room you're forever straightening, and the recognition underneath — that you can tell what counts — goes unread.
Some of what's finished hasn't been counted. Think of one ending, and before you reach ahead, count what it gave you: three things, small and specific. That's the patient side of the wait. If three don't come quickly, take that as news rather than a failure, and nothing is owed to the exercise either way. The yield is sitting there.
cells.sheetLine: The feeling is waiting for next, and the now goes uncounted.
cells.verb: sitting with what the heart knows before moving
cells.place: the quiet room where you recognize what matters before you can explain it

cells.tense: The feeling rested at some earlier point, and you are still standing outside the room it settled in.
cells.act: reconcile what you know with what you feel about it
cells.ask: Take a thing you know to be true and set it beside how you actually feel. Write the single line where the two of them meet, then leave it for the day.
cells.core:
The feeling went quiet. You can still tell what counts when you look, but what you find doesn't land in the present — it sits at the distance of something already handled. What reads as calm is closer to a room you left, and calm isn't something a person can decide to have.
What you know and what you feel have drifted apart, and they can be brought into one line. Take a thing you know to be true and set it beside how you actually feel; write the single line where they meet. Do it once, then leave it for the day. Nothing in the feeling needs forcing — the line is enough to stand on while the rest returns.
cells.sheetLine: You still know what matters. It stays at a distance.

cells.place: the quiet room where you recognize what matters before you can explain it

cells.tense: The recognition is doing its work through you while you credit the mood of the room.
cells.act: read the hardest page of it twice, slowly, before you stop
cells.ask: Find a hard passage — a real page, or something you're living — and give it a second slow read before you put it down. Notice how much of it you already understand.
cells.core:
Something in you reads a room before anyone speaks, and that reading is how you know what counts. Asked about it, you'd say the room just settled, or the timing was lucky. The perception sees through to what's at stake, and the way you account for it keeps that out of the frame.
The depth is already yours; you just don't count it as yours. Find a hard passage — a real page, or something you're carrying — and give it a second slow read before you put it down. You'll see how much of it you already understand. That second pass has an author, and the author is you.
cells.sheetLine: What you call the mood of the room is you.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person's felt life has the depth and steadiness the record attributes to this signature at Balanced and Unacknowledged; the record licenses the capacity, not the biography, so the cells describe the mechanism rather than assert what anyone has lived. The reader could reasonably say the feeling in their chest is not peace but numbness, so the Too Little cell locates them at a door they are standing outside rather than naming any cause. The asks survive being wrong: reading the hardest page twice, counting what an ending gave, and bringing two sides into one plan all work regardless of whether the diagnosis is right. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is in the Unacknowledged cell, where it would be easy to flatter the one who keeps the peace — it has been cut to the plain act of noticing, and nothing else.
